intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene (601906) on chromosome 12q13.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene.
checks.evidence_quote: a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation (p.R332W) in all affected individuals but the atypical case
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a homozygous WNT10B mutation in autosomal recessive SHFM. 'SHFM6' is the OMIM label for this form.

checks.claim: The WNT10B gene is located on chromosome 12q13.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified by homozygosity mapping a novel SHFM locus at 12q13.11-q13 with a maximum multipoint lod score of 5.47 and by subsequent candidate gene approach a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation
checks.explanation: WNT10B was identified as a candidate gene within the 12q13 locus.

paragraphs.text: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is an autosomal recessive form of SHFM. Affected individuals have central reductions of the feet, with or without involvement of the hands (Ugur and Tolun, 2008). Gul and Oktenli (2002) noted that most familial SHFM is autosomal dominant. Kantaputra et al. (2018) suggested that sparse hair and interrupted eyebrows may be associated findings.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is an autosomal recessive form of SHFM.
checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large consanguineous kindred afflicted with autosomal recessive SHFM.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes this form as autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: Individuals affected with SHFM6 have central reductions of the feet, with or without involvement of the hands.
checks.evidence_quote: Twelve affected members had central feet reductions with or without hand involvement
checks.explanation: States the feet and hand findings directly.

checks.claim: Most familial split-hand/foot malformation is autosomal dominant.
checks.evidence_quote: The majority of the familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

checks.claim: Sparse hair and interrupted eyebrows may be associated findings of SHFM6.
checks.evidence_quote: Sparse hair and interrupted eyebrows may be associated findings of SHFM6.

paragraphs.text: Ray (1970) reported split-foot malformation in 2 sibs.

paragraphs.text: Gul and Oktenli (2002) reported 9 individuals with split-hand/split-foot malformation in an inbred kindred. The pattern of malformation varied within the family.

paragraphs.text: Kantaputra et al. (2018) reported an Indian girl with SHFM, sparse hair, and interrupted eyebrows. Unlike some patients with WNT10B variants, the patient and all members of her family had normal bone density and were not obese. The authors suggested that sparse hair and interrupted eyebrows may be associated findings of SHFM6.

paragraphs.text: Verma et al. (1976) concluded that their family, together with earlier reports including that of Freire-Maia (1971), further showed that split-hand and split-foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Their evidence was the occurrence of the deformity in 2 sibships born to first-cousin parents.

checks.claim: Verma et al. (1976) concluded that their family, together with earlier reports including that of Freire-Maia (1971), further showed that split-hand and split-foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.evidence_quote: This report, together with those of Ray (1960) and Freire-Maia (1971), further demonstrates that split-hand and -foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.explanation: The conclusion is stated, and Freire-Maia (1971) is named among the earlier reports. Ray (1960) is also cited, which the draft's word 'including' allows for.

checks.claim: Verma et al. (1976) based their conclusion of autosomal recessive inheritance on the occurrence of split-hand/split-foot deformity in 2 sibships born to first-cousin parents.
checks.evidence_quote: Both the sibship resulted from marriage between first cousins. This report, together with those of Ray (1960) and Freire-Maia (1971), further demonstrates that split-hand and -foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives both the family (2 affected sibships from first-cousin marriages) and the autosomal recessive conclusion. It does not say outright that the conclusion rests on that pattern, so the draft's link between evidence and conclusion is an inference. The reasoning may be spelled out in the full text, which was not supplied.

paragraphs.text: Mufti and Wood (1987) concluded that autosomal recessive inheritance seemed likely, based on the occurrence of ectrodactyly in sisters and half sisters of an extended family.

checks.claim: Mufti and Wood (1987) concluded that autosomal recessive inheritance of ectrodactyly seemed likely, based on its occurrence in sisters and half sisters of an extended family.
checks.evidence_quote: An autosomal recessive gene seems likely to be the mode of inheritance.
checks.explanation: The abstract concludes that autosomal recessive inheritance seems likely. The family it describes is the one with affected sisters and half sisters. The abstract does not spell out the reasoning, but that reasoning follows from the family it describes.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) questioned whether a rare autosomal recessive form of split hand/foot malformation exists. As an alternative, they proposed a two-locus model in which a dominant split hand/foot mutation is controlled by a gene at another locus, and a dominant mutation at that controlling locus causes nonpenetrance of the split hand/foot mutation.

checks.claim: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) questioned whether a rare autosomal recessive form of split hand/foot malformation exists.
checks.evidence_quote: The possibility of the existence of a rare autosomal recessive form of the malformation is discussed
checks.explanation: The title ("Is there an autosomal recessive form...") and the abstract both raise this question.

checks.claim: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) proposed a two-locus model in which a dominant split hand/foot mutation is controlled by a gene at another locus, and a dominant mutation at that controlling locus causes nonpenetrance of the split hand/foot mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: In the two locus model the dominant mutation leading to the split hand/foot malformation is controlled by a gene at another locus. A dominant mutation at the controlling locus leads to non-penetrance of the split hand/foot mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes the two-locus model as stated in the claim.

paragraphs.text: Gul and Oktenli (2002) noted that most familial SHFM is autosomal dominant. For their inbred kindred with 9 affected members, they discussed both autosomal recessive inheritance and a two-locus model.

paragraphs.text: Blattner et al. (2010) concluded that sporadic SHFM is not always a dominant trait and may be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. In that case, the recurrence risk is 25% for sibs and very low for the offspring of patients unless there is consanguinity. They recommended testing patients with sporadic SHFM for WNT10B mutations to determine the recurrence risk.

checks.claim: Blattner et al. (2010) stated that for autosomal recessive SHFM, the recurrence risk is 25% for sibs.

paragraphs.text: Elliott and Evans (2006) noted that split-hand/foot malformation is genetically heterogeneous, with at least 5 loci identified. Using descriptive epidemiology, chi-square analysis, and discriminant function analysis, they identified phenotypic patterns associated with the mapped SHFM loci. They suggested that these patterns could help with classification and with directing mapping efforts and targeted genetic testing.

paragraphs.text: In most affected members of their consanguineous SHFM kindred, Ugur and Tolun (2008) detected a rare insertion variant in the TP63 gene (rs34201045). The variant lies at the alternate promoter used to transcribe the N-terminal-truncated p63 isotype. The authors suggested complex inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Ugur and Tolun (2008) used a candidate gene approach in a large consanguineous kindred with SHFM and identified a homozygous missense mutation in the WNT10B gene (R332W). The mutation was present in all affected individuals except the one with atypical SHFM, and it was also present in an asymptomatic female. The authors proposed that either a second locus contributes to the SHFM phenotype or a suppressor locus prevented the phenotype from appearing in the nonpenetrant female. Most affected members of the kindred also carried a rare insertion variant in TP63 (rs34201045), and the authors suggested complex inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Kantaputra et al. (2018) identified a novel homozygous 3-bp deletion in the WNT10B gene (c.695_697delACA) in an Indian girl with SHFM6. The deletion was predicted to remove asparagine-232 in frame (Asn232del). Protein modeling suggested that the deletion, at a critical position, likely severely affects protein structure and function, likely shortening the protein's lifetime and preventing binding to its receptors and other ligands.
